name: SmartAlbums
tagline: Desktop album design software that turns a folder of client photos into press-ready wedding album spreads.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The core mechanic, drop photos onto a two-page spread, snap them into a grid, export at print resolution with bleed, is very much a weekend build. An agent can give you a local layout canvas, auto-fill from a folder, spread navigation, and a 300 DPI JPEG or PDF export without much drama. What it will not give you is the part photographers actually pay for: hundreds of hand-tuned layout templates, the auto-design pass that makes defensible choices in seconds, and per-lab size and bleed presets that match what the printer expects. Color management for press output is also a real rabbit hole, and your homemade sRGB JPEGs may come back looking nothing like your screen. Build it if you make one album a year for yourself; do not build it if a bad export costs you a client.
coreLoopDIY: A local app that fills photo spreads from a folder using grid templates, lets you nudge and crop each frame, and exports print-resolution spreads as JPEG or PDF.
requirements: A folder of exported JPEGs or TIFFs
Target album spread size, DPI and bleed from your lab's spec sheet
whatYouLose: The large curated template library and the auto-design pass that picks layouts for you
Lab-specific size, bleed and gutter presets that are known to print correctly
Client proofing links and revision round-trips
Color-managed, soft-proofed output with ICC profiles for press
Lightroom and Photoshop round-tripping, plus a maintained desktop app on two operating systems
moatNotes: The moat is not the canvas, it is the thousand small defaults that make a spread look designed and print correctly on a specific lab's press.
whyPeopleStillPay: Album design is billable time, and the people buying this are measuring it in albums per hour, not in features. A tool that auto-designs a 40 page album in a minute and exports files the lab accepts without a reprint pays for itself in one wedding. A personal clone gets you the layout canvas but leaves you doing the design judgment yourself, which is exactly the work you were trying to buy back.
notes: The canvas is easy, the taste is not · budget a test print before you trust your own exporter.
prompt:
Build a local-only album spread designer called "Spreads". No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Node 20 + Express backend, TypeScript.
- React + Vite frontend, TypeScript, plain CSS, no component library.
- sharp for image decoding and print rendering, pdf-lib for PDF assembly, better-sqlite3 for project state.
- Single command: npm run dev starts API on 3001 and UI on 5173.

Core behavior:
1. On startup the user picks a local folder path (typed into the UI, validated server side). The API scans it for .jpg/.jpeg/.tif, reads EXIF capture time with sharp metadata, and builds a photo list sorted chronologically with cached 1200px thumbnails in .cache/.
2. Project settings: spread width and height in inches, DPI (default 300), bleed in inches, gutter in inches. Stored in SQLite.
3. A spread is an ordered list of frames. Ship 12 hardcoded grid templates per spread (1-up full bleed, 2-up, 3-up variants, 4-up, 5-up, 6-up, asymmetric sets) defined as normalized x/y/w/h rectangles. Auto-fill: walk the photo list in order, assign templates in rotation, respecting portrait vs landscape aspect by preferring templates whose frame aspect is closest.
4. Editor canvas: one spread at a time, rendered to scale in the browser with HTML canvas or absolutely positioned img elements. Each frame crops its photo with object-fit cover semantics. User can pan the image inside a frame by dragging and zoom with a slider; store offset and scale per frame. User can swap a frame's photo by dragging a thumbnail from a filmstrip, swap the spread's template, reorder spreads, and add or delete spreads.
5. Export: server-side render each spread at full DPI with sharp (composite each cropped frame onto a white canvas sized width+2*bleed by height+2*bleed), write numbered JPEGs at quality 95 into ./export, and also assemble a single PDF with pdf-lib at the exact trim size with bleed. Draw an optional gutter-safe overlay only in the browser preview, never in the export.

Explicitly out of scope: color management and ICC profiles (document in the README that exports are sRGB and that the user must test print), auto-design beyond the rotation heuristic, client proofing, lab integrations, text and graphic layers, RAW decoding, multi-user anything.

Secrets: none needed. If you add any config, use .env and commit .env.example only.

Deliver a README with the run commands, the data model, a note that all file access is local, and a loud warning that a test print is required before trusting any export.
